changes.before: A vehicle's strongest radio link can lead to a busy computing server, and task admission does not guarantee a result before the deadline. TrafficTwin investigates how infrastructure scheduling affects offered-task deadline attainment under a fixed, pretrained vehicle offloading policy. It separates radio ingress, execution placement, admission and workload reservation. The programme compared seven infrastructure policies in 274 full evaluator runs across five Manchester scenarios; confirmation and follow-up protocols were sealed before their outcomes.
changes.after: TrafficTwin is a research-software platform for configuring, comparing and inspecting vehicular edge-computing studies. This dissertation uses a supplied trace-driven evaluator to ask how infrastructure scheduling affects the proportion of offered tasks meeting their deadlines under a fixed pretrained vehicle policy. Radio ingress, execution placement and admission are treated as separate decisions. Seven infrastructure policies were compared in 274 full evaluator runs across five Manchester scenarios.

changes.before:
Common-target least-workload placement underperformed execution at ingress, whereas causal per-task placement improved attainment in the adaptive incident study, four-draw morning replication and 32-cell confirmation on eight fresh joint fleet/evaluator-seed blocks. In the confirmation, per-task minus ingress was +4.137 percentage points and common-target minus ingress was \ensuremath{-}3.504. Per-task also exceeded causal cyclic spreading by +0.631 points, with a Bonferroni simultaneous 95\% interval of [+0.511, +0.750].

The declared follow-ups found a +0.649-point advantage over the evaluator's two-choice mode. Halving server speed widened the per-task advantage over cyclic spreading by +0.193 points, and a second actor checkpoint preserved the ranking. The full ranking also recurred on weekend, evening-peak and event-night traces of the same network.
changes.after: Common-target least-workload placement underperformed execution at ingress, whereas sequential per-task placement reversed this ranking in incident and morning comparisons. In a sealed confirmation with eight fresh paired fleet/evaluator-seed blocks and four policies, per-task placement improved attainment over ingress by 4.137 percentage points. It also exceeded causal round-robin by 0.631 points, with a Bonferroni simultaneous 95\% interval of [0.511, 0.750]. Thus workload-aware selection added a smaller benefit beyond cyclic spreading.

changes.before: Retrospective analysis links recurring common destinations to shared assignment, queue clearing and deterministic ties. An exact-arithmetic proof establishes when fixed-target reconciliation reproduces sequential admission, while numerical diagnostics show why this guarantee does not extend directly to float32. In the original morning sample, descriptive task accounting locates most gains in reduced gate rejection and also retains individual losses. Separate CPU fixtures show that workload-aware targeting costs more than cyclic spreading, although it runs faster than the common-target implementation in scheduler-only tests.
changes.after: Declared follow-ups found an advantage over two-choice placement, a larger per-task advantage over round-robin at half server speed, and the same ranking with a second actor checkpoint. The ranking also recurred on weekend, evening-peak and event-night traces.

changes.before: The contribution is empirical and analytical evidence about the implementation of established scheduling principles. The findings support a bounded benefit from workload awareness beyond spreading. Generalisation is restricted by two checkpoints sharing one training seed and five scenarios from one demand-scaled Manchester network; global service-work information and aggregate timing further limit physical interpretation. Historical capacity findings retain inconclusive statistics and unresolved scoring uncertainty, which the later gate-enabled results do not resolve.
changes.after: The contribution is a controlled comparison and explanation of how destination selection and workload reservation affect deadline attainment in this evaluator. The findings are limited to the tested model and scenarios from one Manchester network; they do not establish deployed-system performance.

changes.before: Mobility makes this harder. Vehicular radio channels vary quickly \cite{ref5}, and the vehicles around an RSU change while previously admitted work still occupies its server, so RSU loads become uneven \cite{ref7}. Research on heterogeneous vehicular edge computing accordingly considers communication and resource allocation together with stringent latency requirements \cite{ref6}. This motivates examining infrastructure decisions under fixed vehicle-policy weights.
changes.after: Mobility makes this harder. Vehicular radio channels vary quickly \cite{ref5}. Meanwhile, the vehicles around each RSU change while previously admitted work remains queued, producing uneven server loads \cite{ref7}. Vehicular edge-computing research therefore considers communication and resource allocation jointly under latency requirements \cite{ref6}.

changes.before: The \textbf{ingress RSU} is the roadside unit through which a vehicle reaches the infrastructure. TrafficTwin chooses ingress using the strongest simulated radio link. \textbf{Execution placement} is the subsequent choice of server for the task. Keeping execution at ingress avoids logical forwarding, but strong radio quality says nothing about that server's backlog. Assigning the work to another RSU can reduce waiting while introducing a different information and coordination requirement. Figure~\ref{fig:1} shows the decision boundary studied here: the vehicle selects an offloading mode, while the infrastructure resolves the execution destination and admission \hyperref[source-s4]{[S4]}.
changes.after: TrafficTwin is the research-software platform developed for this project around a supplied trace-driven VEC evaluator. Its inherited \texttt{vec\_env} environment selects the \textbf{ingress RSU}, the roadside entry point, using the strongest simulated radio link. \textbf{Execution placement} then selects the server that will process an admitted task. Keeping execution at ingress avoids forwarding, but strong radio quality does not imply a short server backlog. Figure~\ref{fig:1} distinguishes actor mode selection, environmental radio targeting, and infrastructure placement and admission \hyperref[source-s4]{[S4]}.

changes.before: Admission is distinct from timely completion. A finite waiting room may have space for a task even when the queued work would make it late. TrafficTwin's deadline-aware gate supplements the task-count limit by inspecting backlog, but still permits some admitted tasks to miss their deadlines. Rejected tasks therefore remain in the offered population: measuring success only among admitted tasks would allow selective rejection to change the population being compared.
changes.after: Admission is distinct from timely completion. In addition to a task-count limit, the inherited evaluator rejects a candidate when service work already ahead of it is at least its deadline. This backlog-only gate excludes the task's own processing and communication, so admitted tasks may still finish late. All offered tasks remain in the outcome denominator, preventing selective rejection from hiding unsuccessful work.

changes.before: \textbf{Attribution and simulation validity.} Sargent distinguishes verification of a computer model from operational validation for its intended application \cite{ref21}. TrafficTwin's conservation and replay checks primarily establish the former; observed physical RSU service and network measurements would be needed for stronger deployment claims. SUMO supplies a microscopic simulation framework \cite{ref22}, but importing its trajectories does not independently validate a coupled radio/computing model.
changes.after: \textbf{Simulation validity.} Conservation and replay checks verify implementation of the stated model; validation for deployment would additionally require comparison with measured system behaviour \cite{ref21}. SUMO supplies the traffic simulation framework \cite{ref22}, but its trajectories alone do not validate the coupled radio/computing model.
